narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year class ranking, which placed you in the second decile. This low standing relative to your peers pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking in the second decile also contributed to the negative outlook, though with less force. In contrast, your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure; however, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 35, family income in the middle bracket, full-time study plans, gender, and race played only minor roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank improves significantly. Consider retaking the LSAT if possible, and explore academic support programs that target students in the lower deciles. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to your current rejection. (218 words)
